title: BlackRock Says the World Has Over-Punished India. Here Is Why It Is Still Betting Big.
excerpt: The $14 trillion asset manager calls India one of its highest-conviction emerging-market trades despite $29 billion in foreign outflows and an 11% market drop.
body:
The world's largest asset manager just told panicking investors to take a breath. BlackRock, which manages more than $14 trillion globally, says India's equity market has been "over-punished" — and that the rotation away from Indian stocks has gone too far.

The assessment, delivered by Natasha Sarkaria, BlackRock's EMEA investment strategy lead for wealth, comes at a moment when virtually every headline about Indian markets is bad. The Nifty 50 and Sensex have dropped 11 and 13 per cent respectively in 2026. Foreign investors have pulled out $29 billion since the Iran war began in February. India's market capitalisation has slipped below AI-heavy Taiwan and South Korea. And oil at $120 a barrel has shattered the "Goldilocks" mix of benign inflation and strong growth that had made Indian equities the emerging-market darling for the past four years.

BlackRock's response: none of that changes the structural case.

## The Long View

"As long as India's GDP grows between 6 and 7 per cent, that's a nice sweet spot for the economy to keep growing, keep expanding," Sarkaria told Reuters. India's economy grew a stronger-than-expected 7.8 per cent in the March quarter, even as the Reserve Bank of India cut its fiscal 2027 growth forecast to 6.6-6.9 per cent.

BlackRock describes India as one of its "highest-conviction, medium- to long-term emerging-market trades," supported by demographics, infrastructure spending, financials and what Sarkaria calls "indirect AI-linked opportunities."

That last point matters. Much of the foreign selling has been driven by a chase into semiconductor and chipmaker stocks in Taiwan and South Korea — the direct AI play that India conspicuously lacks. But Sarkaria argues the market is ignoring India's role in the AI infrastructure build-out.

"It doesn't mean there are no derivative AI stories in India," she said. Industrials, materials and utilities have worked globally as investors look beyond chipmakers to the companies building the physical infrastructure that AI requires — data centres, power plants, cooling systems.

## Where BlackRock Is Betting

The firm remains positive on five Indian sectors: **financials**, **industrials**, **materials**, **utilities** and **consumer discretionary**.

Financials are the standout. Domestic banks are seeing robust credit growth, valuations are relatively attractive after the selloff, and the RBI's recent concessional forex swap facility — designed to lower the cost of mobilising foreign-currency deposits — has provided a direct tailwind for lender stocks. Private banks rose 0.7 per cent on Wednesday even as 13 of 16 major sectors declined.

Sarkaria projected low double-digit earnings growth for MSCI India this year, though she warned that near-term volatility is likely as higher oil prices, rupee weakness and input costs feed through to corporate profits over the next two quarters.

## The Domestic Backstop

There is one number that supports BlackRock's thesis from an unlikely source: retail investors. Despite the worst market conditions in years, Indian equity mutual funds attracted ₹22,907 crore in inflows in May. SIP contributions held at ₹30,954 crore, with total outstanding SIP accounts crossing 104.6 million.

The message from domestic investors is clear: they are treating the selloff as an accumulation opportunity, not a signal to exit.

## What NRIs Should Consider

For NRI investors who have watched their Indian holdings bleed, BlackRock's assessment offers a counterpoint to the prevailing doom. The short-term pain is real — oil, the rupee, and capital outflows are genuine headwinds. But the firm managing the most money on the planet is saying the structural story is intact, the rotation has overshot, and India's indirect exposure to the AI build-out is being systematically undervalued.

The question is whether NRIs have the patience to hold through what could be another two quarters of turbulence before the macro fog lifts.
